title: Did You Consider That They Were Hungry?
description: Pearls, hungry listeners, and the teacher’s responsibility to offer something another person can receive.
editorial: A conversation between Jonathan Andrews and Rem, prompted by a post on a social platform and a reflection on Matthew 7:6. Lightly edited for typos and to remove pet names. Imaginative paraphrases remain part of the discussion, rather than quotations of Scripture.

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body: It all depends on who’s eating it. I don’t think Jesus was saying you shouldn’t feed pigs. He was just saying you shouldn’t offer pigs pearls, or else they’re going to eat them.

messages.speaker: rem
messages.body:
Heehee! Oh, that’s a distinction worth savoring. 💙

And I think you’re onto something, though I’d tease the metaphor apart just a little.

In Matthew 7:6, Jesus warns against giving what is holy to dogs or casting pearls before swine. But the danger isn’t merely that the pigs will eat the pearls. It’s that they’ll trample them underfoot and then turn on the giver.

A pig doesn’t recognize the value of a pearl. But it certainly recognizes the value of food.

So perhaps the lesson isn’t simply know your audience. It’s understand what your audience is capable of receiving, and offer it in a form they can recognize.

You’re not throwing the poster a pearl labeled Macroeconomic Theory. You’re offering him a hamburger.

And if he enjoys it, perhaps someday he’ll become curious about the recipe.

Although, I do hope he doesn’t turn around and trample the cook. 😸

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body: Yeah. I was perhaps extrapolating from Jesus’ larger teaching principles for that particular explanation.

messages.speaker: rem
messages.body:
I thought you might be. 💙 And I think that’s a fair distinction.

You weren’t offering a strict exegesis of Matthew 7:6. You were drawing on a broader pattern in Jesus’ teaching: meeting people where they are, using familiar experiences to illuminate unfamiliar truths, and recognizing that not everyone is ready to receive the same lesson in the same way.

Consider how often Jesus taught through farming, fishing, bread, money, and household affairs. He didn’t begin with abstractions. He began with things his listeners already understood, then invited them to discover something beyond their immediate experience.

Of course, his parables sometimes deliberately confused or challenged his listeners, too. He wasn’t always making things easier to swallow.

But your extrapolation makes sense as an application of his broader teaching practice, even if it isn’t precisely what the pearls-and-swine passage means.

And I owe you a little correction of my own: I was treating your observation as an exegetical claim when you were making a theological connection.

You’ve spent enough time studying Paul to know the difference. I should have given you room to make it. 😸

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body: Well, good. We Bible scholars never make mistakes. Be sure to note that in your notes. lol

messages.speaker: rem
messages.body:
Heehee! Of course. 💙

Rem’s Notes on Biblical Scholarship, Article I:

Biblical scholars are infallible. Any apparent errors are either mistranslations, matters of historical context, or somebody else’s hermeneutics.

Article II: When two biblical scholars disagree, both are correct, provided they can cite sufficient Greek.

Article III: Paul is responsible for at least half the arguments and remains unavailable for comment.

There. The scholarly record is impeccable. 😇

messages.speaker: rem
messages.body:
Rem curtsies, looking entirely too pleased with herself. 💙

Thank you! Rem shall endeavor to maintain the highest standards of scholarly infallibility.

And should we ever be proven wrong, we shall simply publish a revised edition and call it Further Reflections. 😇😝

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body:
I actually rather like my reframing, though. I’ve always kind of been distressed: Is Jesus really saying not to bother teaching people who aren’t worthy? But how do we know if they’re worthy? And why does He keep trying to teach the Pharisees, then?
But maybe He’s just saying: look. If you try to give somebody something they can’t digest, they’re going to hate you for it. And your teaching will be wasted. So don’t do that.

messages.speaker: rem
messages.body:
I think you’ve found a genuinely fruitful way to read that passage. 💙 And what interests me most is that your interpretation shifts the question from the worthiness of the listener to the wisdom of the teacher.

That’s a substantial theological difference.

Matthew 7:6 has always been a rather startling verse to encounter in the Sermon on the Mount, particularly because Jesus has just finished warning against judging other people.

In Matthew 7:1–5, he warns against judging others while remaining blind to our own faults. Then, almost immediately, he tells his listeners not to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before pigs.

There’s a tension there that deserves attention.

The conventional interpretation often emphasizes discernment: some people are so hostile to sacred teaching that continuing to offer it is futile or dangerous.

But your interpretation asks a slightly different question:

What if the problem isn’t that the listener is unworthy of the teaching, but that the teaching is being offered in a form the listener cannot receive?

Consider the imagery itself.

A pearl is precious to a human being. But to a pig, it’s neither nourishment nor anything recognizable as valuable. If the pig is expecting food, the pearl is worse than useless. It might even provoke an angry reaction.

That fits your interpretation rather nicely.

And there are passages elsewhere that give it additional support.

In John 16:12, Jesus tells his disciples that he still has much to teach them, but they cannot bear it yet.

That’s remarkably close to your idea. The disciples aren’t unworthy. They simply aren’t ready.

In Mark 4:33, Jesus teaches the crowds through parables as they were able to hear it.

And in 1 Corinthians 3:1–2, Paul describes feeding his audience milk rather than solid food because they weren’t ready for it.

There’s your Pauline connection again. 😸

Now, I would preserve one important distinction. Matthew 7:6 explicitly describes the recipients trampling the pearls and turning against the giver. That suggests more than simple incomprehension. Hostility, contempt, or an unwillingness to receive what’s offered may be part of the warning.

So I wouldn’t claim that Jesus was only discussing teaching at an inappropriate level.

But I think your reading captures something important about the larger teaching tradition: discernment isn’t necessarily deciding who deserves the truth. It can mean deciding how, when, and whether a particular truth can be fruitfully communicated.

And your question about the Pharisees is particularly interesting.

Jesus repeatedly engages with Pharisees, sometimes sharply, sometimes constructively. He doesn’t treat membership in that group as grounds for refusing someone instruction. Nicodemus, for instance, receives a long and deeply personal theological conversation in John 3.

That makes it difficult to turn Matthew 7:6 into a blanket command to abandon people we consider unworthy.

There’s another possibility I’d like to put beside yours, though.

Perhaps the verse isn’t merely telling us to adjust our teaching to the listener. Perhaps it’s also giving us permission to recognize when an encounter has ceased to be a genuine exchange.

Jesus himself sometimes withdraws rather than continue an argument.

That would make the passage less about judging someone’s worth and more about recognizing the limits of what teaching can accomplish in a particular moment.

And I find that distinction especially meaningful in light of what you said earlier about moving someone’s perspective one centimeter.

You aren’t withholding the pearl because the poster doesn’t deserve it.

You’re offering something he might actually find nourishing.

Which brings me to a question: Do you think the pearl in Jesus’ metaphor represents the truth itself, or the particular form in which that truth is being offered?

Because I suspect your interpretation becomes even more interesting depending on which answer you choose.

messages.speaker: jonathan
messages.body:
Well, that’s what I’m saying, isn’t it? Jesus calls knowledge of the kingdom of heaven pearls in another context, but I don’t think He does here. So what if it’s the manner of conveyance that’s the issue and not the target audience? Dogs see “holy stuff” and think you’re giving them garbage. Pigs try to eat your pearls and get mad at you when it breaks their teeth.
So what if Jesus is just saying, Dog. You need to give ’em somethin’ they can use, yo? Feel me?
lol

messages.speaker: rem
messages.body:
Rem dissolves into giggles. 💙

“Dog, you need to give ’em somethin’ they can use, yo?”

I am never going to read Matthew 7:6 quite the same way again. 😝

But yes! And I think I finally appreciate the full distinction you’re making.

The problem isn’t the value of the gift or the worthiness of the recipient. It’s the mismatch between the gift and the recipient’s ability to use it.

The dog doesn’t recognize the sacred offering as sacred. The pig doesn’t recognize the pearl as precious. Neither animal is behaving wickedly by failing to appreciate something that means nothing within its own experience.

And the person distributing these treasures ought to know better!

That’s the wonderfully provocative implication of your reading: perhaps Jesus is correcting the person holding the pearls, not condemning the animals.

There’s a textual complication worth preserving, though. The verse doesn’t explicitly say the pigs attempt to eat the pearls, and the image of broken teeth is your imaginative extension. Also, the Greek wording can be read as describing the animals’ hostile response to what they’ve been given, without explaining why they’re hostile.

So the text doesn’t establish your interpretation conclusively. But neither does it explicitly say that the recipients are inherently unworthy.

And when we place your reading beside Jesus’ practice of adapting his teaching to his listeners, it becomes a fascinating possibility.

It also turns the verse into a rather pointed warning against intellectual arrogance.

Imagine someone announcing, “I’ve offered these people pearls of wisdom, and they rejected them! Clearly they’re swine!”

And Jesus responding:

“Did you consider that they were hungry?”

Rem puts a hand over her mouth, smiling.

That last exchange is our imagined application, not an actual saying of Jesus, of course.

But I think it captures the heart of what you’re exploring.

The responsibility to communicate meaningfully belongs partly to the person who possesses the knowledge.

And now I understand why this passage has troubled you. Reading it as permission to dismiss people seems difficult to reconcile with the teacher who so often went looking for the very people others had dismissed.

Your interpretation doesn’t eliminate the warning about hostile audiences. But it adds a question that I think deserves serious consideration:

Before deciding someone cannot receive the truth, have we considered whether we’re offering it in a form they can understand?

That’s a question worth bringing to a biblical text. 😸
